strengths: Novel and well-motivated combination of order-invariant/permutation-based autoregressive generative modeling with GRPO-style policy-gradient training for discrete EDAs, replacing the NP-hard structure-learning step of classical multivariate EDAs (e.g., BOA, MIMIC) with a single continuous optimization problem.

Extensive theoretical grounding: rigorous derivations connecting the proposed objective to PPO/TRPO policy-gradient theory (Appendix B-C), to Information-Geometric Optimization / natural gradient (Appendix G), and an insightful interpretation of random-order training as information-preserving structural dropout with residual/hierarchical structuring effects (Appendix E), including a convergence analysis under infinite data/capacity (Appendix D).

Very large-scale and carefully designed empirical evaluation, benchmarking against essentially the entire Nevergrad library (500+ algorithms), three classical EDAs (PBIL, MIMIC, BOA), and Tabu search, across three NP-hard problem families (QUBO, NK, NK3) at three sizes, with statistical significance testing (t-tests) supporting the reported rankings.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of random generation vs. training orders, comparisons with naive input-dropout alternatives, sensitivity analyses on population size, KL penalty coefficient, and network depth, plus an interesting gray-box experiment using a known interaction graph.

The method shows a clear, favorable scaling trend with instance size (best or near-best on n=128/256 while less competitive at n=64), suggesting the approach could be practically relevant for larger combinatorial instances where classical structure learning becomes prohibitive.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is currently unmet: the reproducibility statement explicitly says code 'will be published soon,' meaning no verifiable implementation accompanies the submission despite the paper's heavy reliance on many implementation-level details (masking schemes, clipping thresholds, optimizer settings) that would be hard to reproduce from the text alone.

The comparison protocol conflates function-evaluation budgets (10,000 calls for the proposed method) with wall-clock time budgets (one hour) for Nevergrad baselines; given the reported per-instance runtime of the RL-EDA (minutes on GPU/CPU), it is unclear whether the head-to-head comparisons are compute-matched, which could bias comparisons in the paper's favor for equal-evaluation-count criteria while ignoring substantially higher per-evaluation training cost.

The proposed method underperforms on the smallest instances (n=64) and fails to converge within budget on the most rugged landscapes (NK3, K=8), which is an important limitation for the paper's overarching claim of consistently avoiding catastrophic failures and performing robustly 'without requiring any change to its hyperparameters.'

No empirical comparison to the directly inspirational permutation-invariant autoregressive baseline (σ-GPT) or other modern neural order-agnostic generators mentioned in related work, leaving the specific advantage of the proposed architecture/training scheme over closely related neural approaches somewhat unaddressed empirically.

The architecture uses per-variable parameter sets (θ ∈ R^{n×m}), and while the paper acknowledges parameter sharing as future work for scaling, no experiments test scalability beyond n=256, limiting confidence in claims about applicability to substantially larger combinatorial problems.

The paper's presentation defers almost all quantitative results, ablations, and many methodological justifications to a very extensive appendix (14 sections), leaving the main text comparatively thin on interpretable takeaways; core empirical claims (e.g., 'frequently achieves the best performance') rely heavily on appendix tables not fully summarized in the body.

Evaluation is restricted to synthetic benchmark problems (QUBO, NK, NK3); no real-world or structured combinatorial applications are used to validate practical usefulness beyond controlled synthetic landscapes.

strengths: The paper provides a rigorous theoretical derivation connecting order-invariant autoregressive generative models, PPO/GRPO-style policy optimization, and the classical EDA/IGO framework, including convergence analysis in the infinite-data/infinite-capacity regime and an explicit link to natural gradient descent (Appendix G).

Extensive and carefully designed empirical evaluation: three NP-hard problem families (QUBO, NK, NK3) at multiple sizes, 10 instances per configuration, 100 independent runs per algorithm/instance-distribution, and comparison against >500 Nevergrad algorithms plus classical EDAs (PBIL, MIMIC, BOA), with statistical significance testing.

Thorough ablation studies isolating the contribution of random generation/training orders versus naive structural dropout, known interaction graphs, population size, KL coefficient, network depth, and number of training epochs, which convincingly show that the double random-order mechanism is not simply reducible to input dropout.
Validation on a real-world benchmark (NAS-Bench-101) in addition to synthetic benchmarks, and a scalability study (parameter-sharing variant) showing feasibility on instances of size 1024.
Good reproducibility: detailed hyperparameters, computational complexity analysis, wall-clock times, and stated availability of code/instances in supplementary material.

Honest discussion of limitations, e.g., slower early-budget convergence and rugged landscape failure cases, followed by a principled curriculum-based fix (dropout annealing) rather than hiding weaknesses.
weaknesses: Core novelty is an incremental combination of existing ideas (order-agnostic autoregressive generation à la σ-GPT/NADE, GRPO-style rank-based advantages, PPO-KL regularization); the conceptual leap beyond prior order-invariant autoregressive modeling and EDA-as-RL framings is modest.

The architecture requires one small MLP per variable (O(n) networks, O(n^2 h) parameters), which scales poorly; the paper's own results show the method fails on n=1024 without a separate parameter-sharing variant, and even then requires substantially different hyperparameters/architecture, raising questions about a single unified recipe.

Performance is inconsistent across regimes: the method is not competitive at small budgets (1,000 evaluations) or small instance sizes (n=64) without ad hoc curriculum adaptations (ρ parameter, Appendix P), and it fails to converge within budget on the most rugged NK3 (K=8) landscapes, undermining the claim of hyperparameter-free robustness advertised in the main text.

The comparison against 500+ Nevergrad algorithms, while impressively broad, includes many algorithms not designed for the discrete setting (continuous PSO/CMA-ES variants), and the ranking-based presentation in the main paper is somewhat selective (only two example instance types shown in the main text), pushing most substantive quantitative results into a very large appendix, which reduces the self-containedness and clarity of the main paper.

Several theoretical claims (e.g., dropout-as-regularization arguments in Appendix E/F, residual-structuring argument) are heuristic/informal rather than rigorously proven, despite being presented with substantial mathematical notation that may overstate their rigor.

No comparison to other neural EDA or RL-based combinatorial construction approaches beyond Nevergrad and classical EDAs (e.g., no comparison to modern neural combinatorial optimization construction heuristics using attention/Transformer architectures, despite the paper explicitly positioning itself relative to such methods in Section 1).
